units.translation: It is not fitting to weep or lament.
the ruin of my form, whence it flew upon me, wretched as I am.
whence it reaps a harvest of tears.
See these blows of the heart, whence they come. Thus Hermann for καρδία σέθεν.
he does not know whence the blows of life come.
whence they approved calling the people Kouretes.
Cypris –, whence the dearest things come to mortals. Cf. τόθεν.

ὁθούνεκα [because], about which see what is said in the Thesaurus vol. 3 p. 1059, is contracted from ὅτου ἕνεκα [for which reason], as ούνεκα [because] from οὗ ἕνεκα [for which reason], but by misuse it is used for simple ὅτι [that], as ούνεκα [because] for the same or for ἕνεκα [for the sake of].
There are not a few examples in Sophocles and Euripides, one in Aeschylus Pr. 330: Ζηλῶ σ᾽ ὁθούνεκ᾽ ἐκτὸς αἰτίας κυρεῖς [I envy you because you are free from blame].
For young helmsmen hold sway over Olympus.
For his wits steered his passion, where Porson rightly ψακοστρόφουν.
as a careful helmsman of a ship.
Who then is the helmsman of necessity?
of the tiller, the last guide of the ship.
in the stern of the city, wielding the tiller.
well directing the tiller of his mind.
you left great Oebares (the middle syllable long).
as is right to open one's mouth to friends.
and they do not open the bridal chambers. Scaliger rightly θιγόντι.
to open the house of Artemis nearby.
I know, I know; it is a perfect, which grammarians derive from a fictitious present εἰδέω or εἴδω.

The first and third person common to all writers is οἶδα [I know] and οἶδε or οἶδεν [he knows], second person οἶσθα [you know]. The remaining forms of which examples are found in Aeschylus are the imperative as if from ἴσημι [I know], which grammarians invented, ἴσθι [know] with plural ἴστε [know], subjunctive of the aorist εἰδῶ [I may know], εἰδῇς [you may know], εἰδῇ [he may know], εἰδῶμεν [we may know], optative εἰδείην [I would know], infinitive and participle of the perfect εἰδέναι [to know] and εἰδώς [knowing], εἰδυῖα [knowing], εἰδότες [knowing], εἰδυῖαι [knowing], future middle form εἴσομαι [I will know]. Of the pluperfect ἤδη [I knew] (with plural ᾔδεμεν [we knew]), about the forms of which I have spoken in the Lexicon Sophocleum p. 385, there are no examples in Aeschylus, one of the other form ἦσαν [they knew] for ᾔδεσαν [they knew] Pr. 451 κοὔτε πλινθυφεῖς δόμους προσείλους ἦσαν [nor did they know brick-built houses facing the sun], to which another will be added, if Ag. 1099 Porson rightly corrected ἢ μὴν κλέος σου μαντικόν πεπυσμένοι | ἦσμεν [we had heard your prophetic fame], προφήτας δ᾽οὔτινας ματεύομεν [and we seek no prophets], where in M is read ήμεν, which there is no necessity to change.
About the pluperfect ἦσμεν [we knew] and ἦσαν [they knew] it has been said above.
I know that Zeus is harsh and keeps justice on his own side.
No one, I know well, wishing to babble in vain.
